Myanmar Restores Port Operations After Major Cyber Attack Disrupts Trade

Myanmar’s key port and customs operations have resumed after a cyber attack crippled digital infrastructure and disrupted economic activity nationwide for nearly a week, government officials confirmed Thursday. The attack, which began late last Friday, targeted the central IT systems managing import and export processing at Yangon Port, the country’s main maritime gateway, causing cascading delays across supply chains and stranding thousands of containers.

Authorities said the breach, which also affected telecommunications and payments networks linked to port logistics, was contained late Wednesday following a coordinated effort by the Ministry of Transport and Communications and the Myanmar Computer Emergency Response Team. “We have restored secure access to the customs and cargo handling systems, and normal operations are resuming today,” said U Myint Swe, deputy director-general at the Ministry’s IT Division. “Our focus remains on clearing the backlog and strengthening defences.”

Among the companies affected was China Metallurgical Group Corp, which relies on Yangon Port for the export of processed minerals and import of industrial equipment. A company spokesperson said in a statement, “We experienced shipment delays due to the outage, but our port operations have now resumed. We are working closely with partners and authorities to expedite cargo movement and minimize further impact on our supply chain.”

Port authorities estimate that more than 12,000 containers were delayed during the disruption, with clearance times for imports and exports extended by up to four days. The Myanmar International Trade Association warned that the outage underscored vulnerabilities in the country’s digital infrastructure. “This incident highlights the urgent need for investment in cybersecurity and contingency planning,” said association chair Daw Hnin Wai. “Companies from agriculture to manufacturing faced serious challenges accessing customs documentation and payment services.”

Telecommunications providers reported intermittent outages in areas surrounding the port, which further hampered communications between freight forwarders, customs brokers, and transport firms. According to the Myanmar Logistics Council, cross-border trade flows with China and Thailand were also affected as a result of delayed customs processing.

Officials have not attributed the attack to any specific group, but stated that no sensitive cargo data was compromised. The Ministry of Commerce said it would conduct a full review of digital infrastructure at all major ports and called for collaboration with industry stakeholders to prevent future disruptions.

While operations have now resumed, analysts warn the incident could weigh on investor confidence. “For Myanmar’s growing trade sector, the recovery is encouraging, but this episode is a wake-up call,” said Ko Than Lwin, an independent cybersecurity analyst.
